            Nine indicted over AI server exportsCHINA-BOUND: The nine — including one Nvidia and two Super Micro employees — colluded to ‘illegally export’ servers equipped with advanced chips despite US curbs
  - By Wen-Yee Lee and Ben Blanchard / Reuters
 Nine people, including employees of Nvidia and Super Micro, have been indicted over illegal exports of artificial intelligence (AI) servers to China, the Keelung District Prosecutors’ Office said yesterday. Semiconductor powerhouse Taiwan is the world’s largest producer of advanced chips used in AI applications. Prosecutors this year investigated the suspected illegal export of servers equipped with Nvidia chips subject to US export controls. Washington has imposed curbs since 2022, making it illegal for such semiconductors to be exported or sold in China without a license. The letters AI (artificial intelligence) are placed on a computer motherboard in an illustration on June 23, 2023.Photo: Reuters Eight people, including one employee of Nvidia’s Taiwan unit and two employees of Super Micro’s Taiwan unit, were charged with breach of trust and document forgery in connection with the illegal export of high-end AI servers, Keelung prosecutors said in a statement. Neither company immediately responded to requests for comment. A ninth defendant was charged in a related case involving the alleged siphoning of funds from a distributor company involved, the statement said, without providing the full names of any of the defendants. The alleged scheme involved making it appear that 130 B300 servers ordered from Super Micro would be installed and used at a rented server facility in Taiwan. Prosecutors said false end-user documents stated that the servers would be installed in Taiwan. Of those 130 servers, 74 were ultimately exported and delivered to Chinese customers through routes that included direct shipments to China, as well as transshipments through Indonesia, Japan and Hong Kong, they said. The remaining 56 servers were intended to be exported to a company in Japan, prosecutors said, but Taiwanese customs officials detected irregularities and stopped their export. The prosecutors said the defendants were “fully aware” that Nvidia and Super Micro have “rigorous internal control procedures” regarding exports. However, the defendants “colluded with one another at various levels for enormous profit, illegally exporting high-end servers, increasing corporate compliance costs, and severely damaging our nation’s international image,” they added. Taiwan has tightened export controls in the past few years to keep advanced technology and know-how from reaching China.

items.title: Taipei leads the rise in average life expectancy
items.body_text:
- 
            Taipei leads the rise in average life expectancyLONG LIFE: Taiwan’s average life expectancy of 81.27 was higher than the global average of 73.5, with women outliving men by nearly seven years, official data showed
  - Staff writer, with CNA
 Taiwan’s average life expectancy climbed to 81.27 last year from 80.77 a year earlier, with Taipei recording the longest average at 83.98, the Ministry of the Interior said yesterday. Despite the year-on-year rise, Taiwan’s national average life expectancy had not yet returned to the pre-COVID-19 peak of 81.32 in 2020, the ministry said. However, it is higher than the global average of 73.5, it added. The number of deaths last year moved lower for the third consecutive year, as the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic eased, down 1,674 from a year earlier to 199,639, the ministry said. The number of deaths aged 65 or older was 151,936 last year, accounting for 76.1 percent of the national total. The average crude death rate slid 0.005 percentage points from a year earlier to 0.885 percent, it said. The average life expectancy of women and men in Taiwan rose 0.45 years and 0.51 years from a year earlier to 84.75 and 77.93 respectively, the ministry said. Average life expectancy for women in Taiwan returned to the pre-COVID-19 peak of 84.74 in 2020, but the average among men did not return to 2020’s peak of 78.11, it said. The average for both women and men in Taiwan was higher than the global average of 76.2 years and 70.9 years respectively. Taipei led in average life expectancy, rising from 83.4 in 2024 to 83.98 last year, ahead of Hsinchu City (82.13 years) and New Taipei City (81.54 years). Taitung County had the lowest average life expectancy at 76.49 years. It was the only administrative area in Taiwan to report a figure below 77. Taipei also recorded the highest life expectancy of 86.74 years among women, ahead of Hsinchu City’s 85.2 years. The capital also had the highest average life expectancy of 81.1 years among men, followed by Hsinchu City at 79.1 years. Taitung reported the lowest average life expectancy of 81.54 years for women and 72.3 years for men, the data showed. The latest statistics about individual administrative areas excluded Kinmen County, which saw a large population outflow, and Lienchiang County, the ministry said.

items.title: Heavy rains cause floods, landslides, mass evacuations
items.body_text:
- 
            Heavy rains cause floods, landslides, mass evacuations
  - By Lu Yun-feng / Staff reporter, with CNA
 Heavy rain brought by a low-pressure system and strong southwesterly winds triggered widespread flooding, landslides and damage across central, southern and eastern Taiwan yesterday, disrupting travel and prompting mass evacuations. As of 6pm yesterday, torrential rains had left one person dead in Tainan, four missing — one each in Tainan and Pingtung County and two in Hualien County — and 155 injured nationwide, the Central Emergency Operation Center said. The center added that 4,263 people were evacuated across the nation: 2,649 in Kaohsiung, 765 in Pingtung County, 567 in Tainan, 224 in Hualien County, 46 in Taitung County and 12 in Chiayi County. Firefighters use an inflatable boat to transport people to An Nan Hospital in Tainan yesterday.Photo courtesy of a member of the public In Kaohsiung, continuous downpours caused roads to collapse in Cianjhen (前鎮), Renwu (仁武) and Gangshan (岡山) districts, including a sinkhole 3m long, 2m wide and 1.2m deep on Cianjhen’s Guangsi Road. In Tianliao District (田寮), a landslide on a road near Neian Bridge on Sunday afternoon left more than 30 residents temporarily stranded before clearance operations began. Pingtung County reported severe urban and agricultural flooding, particularly in Wandan (萬丹), Chaojhou (潮州) and Donggang (東港) townships, where water levels reached thigh-high on several major roads. A vehicle is trapped at a section of Nansi 115 Road in Tainan’s Lioujia District yesterday after days of torrential rain damaged roads in the area.Photo courtesy of the Lioujia District Office In Tainan, 24-hour accumulated rainfall exceeded 400mm in Yongkang (永康) and Rende (仁德) districts. Rising water levels along the Sanye River (三爺溪) caused flooding in low-lying areas, forcing the temporary closure of both ramps to Rende Interchange on Freeway No. 1. As the roads near An Nan Hospital were also inundated, firefighters used inflatable boats to transport about 200 people seeking medical treatment. Continuous rain also caused a side wall of the Great East Gate, a national historic site constructed in 1725, to collapse early yesterday morning after rainwater seeped into its base. In Hualien County, several southern townships recorded more than 300mm of rainfall, and surging water in the Siouguluan River (秀姑巒溪) washed away the temporary Yuchang access road connecting Yuli (玉里) and Changliang (長良). Firefighters were searching for a hospital security guard who was reported missing after his mobile phone signal was last detected near the crossing. Authorities also closed several mountain roads and temporary bridge crossings in southern Hualien as a precaution. Nearby, at the Wanli River (萬里溪) barrier lake, the water level dropped by 4.7m, reducing its volume by about 1 million tonnes. Nonetheless, authorities maintained a red alert for the river channel. All 209 people in the evacuation zone around the river landslide-dammed lake have been evacuated. Heavy rain is forecast to continue across most of the country through this morning, with torrential rainfall likely in the southern and southeastern areas due to strong southwesterly winds and multiple weather systems, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said. As Typhoon Saudel continues to move toward Taiwan, a sea warning might be issued tomorrow, it said. Saudel is forecast to approach the Ryukyu Islands tomorrow before turning southwest and passing close to Taiwan on Thursday and Friday, it said. While the center has a low probability of making landfall in Taiwan, its storm circulation would affect northern Taiwan and the Matsu Islands (Lienchiang County), it said. Another tropical storm, Atsani, which formed southeast of the Philippines at 8am yesterday, is expected to be absorbed into Saudel’s circulation, the agency said. A third storm, Narra, near Vietnam yesterday, is not expected to directly affect Taiwan, the CWA said.

items.title: Chinese ambassador begins Australia posting, says took bus to work
items.summary: Chinese ambassador Liu Jinsong said he had taken a public bus in Australia and spoke with “ordinary” people on his way to his new posting in the capital Canberra. Liu arrived in Australia on Monday, saying in a statement on the embassy website that he felt “both honoured and deeply conscious of the responsibility”. He […]
items.body_text:
Chinese ambassador begins Australia posting, says took bus to work
China’s new ambassador to Australia Liu Jinsong said he took the bus from Sydney to Canberra, where he had chatted “with ordinary Australians on board, and thoroughly enjoyed the experience.”
Chinese ambassador Liu Jinsong said he had taken a public bus in Australia and spoke with “ordinary” people on his way to his new posting in the capital Canberra.
Liu arrived in Australia on Monday, saying in a statement on the embassy website that he felt “both honoured and deeply conscious of the responsibility”.
He said he had taken the bus from Sydney to Canberra, where he had chatted “with ordinary Australians on board, and thoroughly enjoyed the experience”.
Relations between Beijing and Canberra reached a low point under former prime minister Scott Morrison, as China slapped import bans and restrictions on Australian commodities including coal, barley and wine.
Several Australian moves had angered China, including legislation against overseas influence operations, barring tech giant Huawei from 5G contracts, and calling for an independent investigation into the origins of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Ties have seen a marked improvement under Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who has visited Beijing twice since taking office in 2022.
But sources of tensions remain. Last month, Australia condemned China’s test of a nuclear-capable missile in the South Pacific, calling the launch “destabilising”.
China remains the biggest customer for Australia’s iron ore, but Canberra has upped scrutiny of Chinese investment in the rare earths sector.
Liu on Monday said “both sides should respect each other’s core interests and major concerns”.
“Our two countries have no historical grievances, no fundamental conflict of interests, highly complementary economies and mutually enriching cultures”.
Liu replaces Xiao Qian, an outspoken diplomat who often drew headlines in Australia for sometimes-fiery rhetoric defending the party line.
Liu previously served as head of the foreign ministry’s Department of Asian Affairs, during which he held high-profile negotiations with Japanese officials as a diplomatic row erupted over Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s comments on Taiwan.

items.title: Six-company consortium wins Northern Metropolis tender for HK$1.03 billion
items.summary: A consortium of mainland Chinese firms and a local property company has been awarded a HK$1.03 billion tender for the first major land parcel to be developed as part of the Northern Metropolis mega project in the northern New Territories. However, the fact that the consortium will operate only one of the three tech parks […]
items.body_text:
A consortium of mainland Chinese firms and a local property company has been awarded a HK$1.03 billion tender for the first major land parcel to be developed as part of the Northern Metropolis mega project in the northern New Territories.
However, the fact that the consortium will operate only one of the three tech parks on the plot, with the government to oversee the others, may indicate that the market remains “cautious” about investing in the infrastructure project, a former lawmaker said.
The six enterprises, consisting of both state-owned and private firms, have projected an investment of about HK$16.8 billion in the Hung Shui Kiu/Ha Tsuen New Development Area, which is expected to create 6,000 jobs and provide 3,000 residential flats, according to a Monday statement.
The six-company joint venture, HSK New Development, comprises subsidiaries of China Overseas Land & Investment, China Merchants Land, China Resources Land (Overseas), China Tourism Group, and e-commerce giant JD.com, as well as Hong Kong developer Sino Land.
The 11-hectare Hung Shui Kiu/Ha Tsuen site is the first “large-scale land disposal” in the Northern Metropolis to be tendered. Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn said in the Monday statement that the plot “is a project of considerable scale with a long investment period.”
“The consortium of successful tenderers encompasses not only major enterprises that have long participated in local real estate development, but also market leaders that are well-established in other industries with undeniable experience and capability,” Linn said.
The firms had pooled their strengths to “cast a vote of confidence” in the Northern Metropolis, she said.
The Northern Metropolis is a sprawling infrastructure project set to transform 30,000 hectares of land in rural Hong Kong near the border with mainland China into a tech hub, providing more homes and deepening the city’s integration with neighbouring Shenzhen.
The government adopted a “two-envelope” system when assessing the tenders, with a 30 per cent weighting for bids’ monetary value and 70 per cent for non-monetary benefits such as creating jobs and bringing in high-quality enterprises.
Remaining cautious
The joint venture will be responsible for developing three residential sites that can yield about 3,000 flats, as well as an Enterprise and Technology Park. They will be granted to the consortium on 50-year leases.
The consortium will also build a large-scale modern logistics hub within the park, with e-commerce titan JD.com positioned as the anchor tenant.
HSK New Development will also complete site formation works for two other tech parks totalling 4.5 hectares, though their development and operation will be conducted by the government via a firm set up for this project, the Hung Shui Kiu Industry Park Company.
The winning bidder will also be responsible for getting another plot spade-ready for government use. Site formation works should be completed, and the plot returned to the government, by the end of 2028.
In a Facebook post, former lawmaker Edward Lau said that the tender result provides “clear evidence” of a vote of confidence in the Northern Metropolis. But he also noted that only one of the three tech park sites would be managed by the consortium, indicating that the market “remains cautious” about long-term investment.
Lau Chun-kong, chair of the Land Policy Panel at the Hong Kong Institute of Surveyors, said on an RTHK radio programme on Tuesday that the consortium assuming responsibility for one tech park site is a positive outcome.

items.title: Woman arrested for alleged sedition outside court ahead of Tiananmen vigil group’s national security case verdict
items.summary: Hong Kong police arrested a woman for alleged sedition outside the West Kowloon Law Courts Building on Friday, hours before leaders of a Tiananmen vigil group were found guilty under the national security law. Police told local media outlets that a 45-year-old was arrested early on Friday on suspicion of acting with seditious intention, disorder […]
items.body_text:
Hong Kong police arrested a woman for alleged sedition outside the West Kowloon Law Courts Building on Friday, hours before leaders of a Tiananmen vigil group were found guilty under the national security law.
Police told local media outlets that a 45-year-old was arrested early on Friday on suspicion of acting with seditious intention, disorder in public places, and obstructing police.
She was detained for investigation.
According to The Collective, the woman was among those queueing for seats in the public gallery for the verdict for Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan. The two are former leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, which used to organise Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen vigils.
The organisation itself, which announced its disbandment in September 2021, was also on trial.
Both the two activists and the Alliance were accused of inciting subversion through calls for “ending one-party rule” – a slogan that prosecutors said amounted to calling for the overthrow of the Chinese Communist Party.
The woman was taken into a police vehicle at around 5am, according to The Collective.
A witness who was also in the queue told the media outlet that the woman was wearing a black t-shirt with Japanese characters.
HKFP has reached out to the police for comment.
Acting with seditious intention is an offence under Article 23, the city’s local security law. It is punishable by up to seven years’ imprisonment, or 10 years if the offence is committed with foreign forces.
The Alliance case was adjourned to Friday for mitigation statements.

items.body_text:
Why is Xiaomi doubling down on in-house chips despite profit slump?
Chinese tech giant’s Xring O3 3nm AI processor scheduled to debut aboard folding smartphone in September
Xiaomi’s long-term push into proprietary silicon is laying the groundwork for complex artificial intelligence workloads on smartphones and cars, analysts say, as the Chinese tech giant doubles down on self-developed chips despite an earnings slump and soaring component costs.
On Monday it unveiled its flagship Xring O3 3-nanometre AI processor for smartphones, which is scheduled to debut in September aboard its Xiaomi 18 Fold smartphone.
The company has also introduced the Xring O100 – a 6nm AI accelerator designed to boost Xiaomi’s MiMo large language model when paired with the O3 – alongside a 3nm Xring D100 chip for autonomous driving. Xiaomi said both the O100 and D100 will be deployed commercially next year.
Ivan Lam, a senior analyst at Counterpoint Research, said Xiaomi’s semiconductor progress placed it in “the top tier of China’s self-developed mobile systems-on-a-chip (SoC)”.
“In the current age of AI, on-chip AI performance has become even more critical as AI workloads are becoming more complex,” Lam said, adding that while semiconductor investments yielded no immediate financial returns, Xiaomi’s long-term commitment remained positive.
Xiaomi’s chip expansion comes as the global smartphone industry grapples with surging memory and component costs, squeezing profit margins across handsets and electric vehicles.

items.body_text:
‘Children were in pieces’: memories still raw 6 months after Iran school strike
Families grieve at least 155 killed in US-linked Tomahawk missile attack on Minab school during opening hours of war
For months, Masoumeh Zakeri has endlessly replayed the last night she spent with her nine-year-old daughter before she was killed in a strike on her school during the opening hours of the US-Israel war with Iran.
Motahreh excitedly talked about coming holidays, planned weddings and the clothes she wanted to buy. She had a Ramadan pre-fast meal shortly before dawn and then Zakeri tucked her into bed.
“I never saw her again. (That was) the last time,” the 44-year-old mother told Agence France-Presse.
Motahreh woke before her parents and took the bus to Shajareh Tayebeh school in Iran’s southern city of Minab. Hours later, the attacks on Iran began and Zakeri received a call telling her to pick up her daughter.
She did not make it in time.
By the time she arrived, the school had been struck, and Motahreh was among at least 155 people killed, most of them children – the deadliest strike yet reported by Iran.

〔體育中心／綜合報導〕日職各隊今天做出人員異動，西武獅台灣強打林安可、樂天金鷲21歲好手陽柏翔，都升上一軍。包含日本火腿21歲新星孫易磊在內，目前旅日台將有3人在一軍舞台。
林安可因左膝疼痛他在8月9日被降至二軍，近期在二軍出賽3場擊出2轟、共9打數敲4安。林安可本季在一軍出賽59場，有6轟、22分打點，打擊三圍是0.228/0.302/0.391，整體攻擊指數（OPS）為0.694。

陽柏翔今年曾在4月10日升上一軍，留下1打數吞三振的成績後，但該月12日後就被登錄抹消。這是陽柏翔相隔4個多月重回一軍舞台。而樂天金鷲今天作客歐力士猛牛，陽柏翔有望出賽。

三菱（Mitsubishi）在 5 月底時宣布創下 7 連霸紀錄，贏得 12 次總冠軍的 Mitsubishi Pajero 將重出江湖，今（25）日在 Pajero 專屬網頁上宣布，Pajero 將於 9 月 2 日進行全球首演，重新將這款經典越野休旅帶回來。
在 Pajero 專屬網頁裡，Mitsubishi 製作一組動畫，透過 Pajero 這六個字母，在裡頭透露這次 Pajero 的各種特點，並且刻意以沙土方式呈現，訴說著 Pajero 一貫的越野本質。
動力則可能採現行 Triton 的 2.4 升渦輪柴油引擎配置，具備 204 匹最大馬力、47.9 公斤米峰值扭力的輸出，滿足越野環境的使用需求。
Mitsubishi 製作一組動畫，透過 Pajero 這六個字母，在裡頭透露這次 Pajero 的各種特點。
字母裡，還刻意以沙土方式呈現，訴說著 Pajero 一貫的越野本質。
Mitsubishi 先前也透過 Star Camp 2026 品牌活動，舉辦大改款 Pajero 搶先賞車會，邀請現行 Pajero 車主及品牌支持者提前一睹大改款 Pajero 風采，而不少看過的人都給出相當高的評價，表示「外型比預期的還酷」、「內裝質感很好，空間也非常大」及「迫不及待想把車開回家」，讓人對於大改款 Pajero 有著更多期待。
Pajero 於 1982 年推出，是品牌標誌性越野 SUV，從 1983 年起參加達卡拉力賽，取得輝煌成績，後來更衍伸出 Pajero mini、Pajero iO 等版本，歷經四代車型，在全球 170 多個國家和地區售出超過 325 萬輛，如今這個品牌越野神主牌再次復活，也象徵著 Mitsubishi 即將重拾當年 Pajero 在達卡拉力賽的輝煌。

items.body_text:
高市幼兒園午餐補助惹議 教師工會籲擴大適用對象
高雄市公幼班導師將納入午餐免費補助對象，教師工會籲擴大適用對象。（資料照）
高市將自115學年度起，公立幼兒園普通班及集中式學前特教班班級導師，比照市立國中小班級導師，由市府全額補助午餐餐費，高雄市教師職業工會雖表肯定，但究竟如何認定補助資格出現混亂，質疑在執行端會產生新的不公平。
高市教師工會幼委會主委楊麓潔指出，幼兒園的午餐照顧，不能直接套用國中小「班級導師」的概念，幼兒因生活自理能力仍在發展，午餐期間不只是陪同用餐，更包含分餐、進食協助、飲食安全、如廁、清潔及午休轉銜等工作，將是幼兒園一天中，最需要團隊共同投入人力的時段之一。
實務上，幼兒園除班級導師外，兼任行政教師、教保員，以及其他教保服務人員，也可能因園所人力配置及輪值方式，實際進入班級協助午餐照顧，若政策僅以「是否掛名班級導師」作為補助標準，就可能出現2人共同照顧同一班幼兒午餐，卻只有其中1人獲得補助的不合理情況。
楊麓潔認為，政策既然是為了支持教師及教保服務人員在午餐時間承擔幼兒照顧與指導工作，補助資格就應回到「實際工作事實」，而非僵化地以職稱或行政編制作為唯一判準。
對於幼兒園午餐補助，高市教師工會提出2點訴求：
一、擴大午餐補助適用對象：補助範圍應由「班級導師」擴及實際參與幼兒午餐照顧及指導的教保服務人員，符合幼兒園團隊共同照顧的實際工作型態。
二、建立明確一致的認定標準：教育局應儘速釐清補助資格，兼任行政或未掛名班級導師者，只要實際、固定承擔午餐時段幼兒照顧與班級支援工作，即應納入補助，避免各園自行解讀，造成同工不同待遇。
高市教師工會強調，幼兒園有不同於國中小的照顧需求，政策不能用「職稱」切割大家共同承擔的工作，誰實際投入幼兒午餐照顧，誰就應獲得相應支持。開學在即，市府既然已跨出值得肯定的第一步，更應把最後一哩路做好，讓午餐補助真正符合幼教現場，而不是讓第一線為了「誰才算午餐指導者」再生爭議。

items.title: As smugglers vanish from North Korea’s border, security agents’ lifestyles take a hit
items.summary: North Korea’s crackdown on smuggling along its border with China has cut off a key source of side income for state security agents who once profited from looking the other way. North Pyongan province security agents who built personal ties with smugglers to earn extra income are now seeing their standard of living slip, a […]
items.body_text:
North Korea’s crackdown on smuggling along its border with China has cut off a key source of side income for state security agents who once profited from looking the other way.
North Pyongan province security agents who built personal ties with smugglers to earn extra income are now seeing their standard of living slip, a Daily NK source in the province said Monday. Smuggling activity has sharply declined in border areas including Uiju county, and the downturn has hit not only the North Korean people who once made a living from the trade, but also the agents who profited alongside them.
“Police officers are directly involved in public security and administrative affairs, so they have plenty of opportunities to make money on the side, but security agents don’t have that,” the source said. “In border areas especially, a large share of their livelihood came from money and goods tied to managing smugglers and smuggling bases. Now that smuggling has been cut off, security agents are taking a direct hit.”
From motorcycles to bicycles
A security agent assigned to a village in Uiju county and his family were frequently seen riding motorcycles or taking taxis just a few months ago, the source said, but lately they have increasingly been spotted on bicycles instead.
Villagers have noticed the shift, saying things like, “It’s completely different from when the smugglers were paying him off,” and “You can tell smugglers aren’t operating anymore just by watching him ride a bike now.”
The village was once home to several smuggling bases and the people connected to them, making it a coveted posting among security agents, the source said. Competition for the assignment was so fierce, given the financial upside, that agents reportedly called in personal connections to secure it.
But as authorities have tightened their crackdown on smuggling over the past two to three months, agents in these once-prized postings have been forced into a far more frugal lifestyle, whether they like it or not.
“In the past, they would casually pull out and smoke good cigarettes, but these days that’s rarely seen,” the source said. “People around them say there’s a clear difference between when smuggling was happening and when it isn’t.”
“Even though living standards here have generally improved compared to the past, there’s a big difference in daily life between people who rely solely on rations and those who bring in occasional side income,” the source added. “That gap shows up everywhere, from a single cigarette to a meal to a means of transportation.”
As Kim Jong Un’s government moves to block smuggling along the border and bring all foreign trade under centralized state control, the long-standing symbiotic relationship between smugglers and security agents appears to be unraveling.
“When smugglers were making money, the security agents connected to them had it easy too, but now that link itself is being severed,” the source said. “It’s not just smugglers who are losing out from this crackdown.”

items.title: North Korea cracks down on ghostwritten graduation theses at Pyongyang universities
items.summary: North Korea’s Cabinet Ministry of Education has ordered major universities in Pyongyang to stamp out the ghostwriting of graduation theses, sparking anxiety among soon-to-graduate students and their faculty advisers, according to a source inside the country. The education ministry issued the directive in mid-August, telling each central university to “thoroughly eliminate” the practice of writing […]
items.body_text:
North Korea’s Cabinet Ministry of Education has ordered major universities in Pyongyang to stamp out the ghostwriting of graduation theses, sparking anxiety among soon-to-graduate students and their faculty advisers, according to a source inside the country.
The education ministry issued the directive in mid-August, telling each central university to “thoroughly eliminate” the practice of writing theses on students’ behalf, a Daily NK source in Pyongyang said Monday. Intensive inspections into how graduating students prepare their theses are expected to run for about a month.
Inspectors are expected to focus on whether students personally chose their thesis topics and took part themselves in gathering research materials and drafting their papers, the source said. For students who have already finished their theses, examiners plan to check whether they understand the material well enough to explain it in their own words.
It remains unclear whether the ministry will lead the inspections directly, hand the task to the Pyongyang city department of education, or have universities cross-check each other’s students, according to the source.
Theses often treated as mere formality
Ghostwriting graduation theses is reportedly common at North Korean universities. Unlike science and engineering-focused schools such as Kim Chaek University of Technology or Pyongyang Medical University, some humanities departments treat a passing thesis as good enough, even without meaningful research, the source said.
“At some liberal arts universities, there’s a strong belief that all that matters is getting the thesis approved, even without any notable research achievement,” the source said. “The thesis is treated as just a formality to earn a diploma, and it’s rare to hear of anyone failing to graduate because of their thesis.”
As a result, some students have prepared for graduation by asking classmates or underclassmen skilled at writing to complete their entire thesis for them, the source said.
With news of the crackdown spreading, universities are anxious about being caught up in the fallout. Ahead of the formal inspections, schools have reportedly begun reviewing graduating students’ thesis preparation on their own. Some are requiring students to document how they gathered materials and drafted their papers, while in certain departments, faculty advisers are holding one-on-one interviews with students to directly confirm their thesis topics and content.
“Students who already received help from someone else, or whose thesis preparation is lacking, are on edge, worried that problems could surface during the university’s internal review,” the source said. “Ghostwriting is not only a problem for students, since the faculty members who supervised the thesis cannot escape responsibility either, so professors are just as on edge.”

items.title: North Korea’s wealthy still crave South Korean cosmetics despite crackdown
items.summary: Demand for South Korean cosmetics among North Korea’s wealthy elite shows no sign of slowing, and smugglers have begun repackaging the products into Chinese containers to slip past increasingly strict customs checks. “Even a passing reference to South Korea can bring punishment in North Korea, but preference for South Korean cosmetics remains high here,” a […]
items.body_text:
Demand for South Korean cosmetics among North Korea’s wealthy elite shows no sign of slowing, and smugglers have begun repackaging the products into Chinese containers to slip past increasingly strict customs checks.
“Even a passing reference to South Korea can bring punishment in North Korea, but preference for South Korean cosmetics remains high here,” a source in Ryanggang province told Daily NK on Friday. “In Hyesan, demand for South Korean cosmetics has recently spread beyond donju to their children as well.” Donju, meaning “masters of money,” is the term for North Korea’s class of merchants and traders who emerged after the country’s economy opened to informal markets.
South Korean cosmetics are expensive and difficult to obtain because of the authorities’ crackdown, so simply using them has become a symbol of economic power, connections and social influence, according to the source.
Among some young people in particular, whether someone uses South Korean cosmetics can significantly shape their relationships, the source explained. Users bond by sharing information on how they obtained the products and their experiences using them, turning South Korean cosmetics into more than a display of wealth: a way of forming their own social circles.
As a result, children of wealthy families ask their parents to get them South Korean cosmetics so they are not left out among their peers, and parents comply regardless of cost to satisfy their children’s demands.
Smugglers adapt as customs tighten
North Korean authorities strictly prohibit the import and distribution of South Korean cosmetics, but traders are using every method available to bring in products because of strong internal demand and the large profits involved, the source said.
“Until now, the main method was simply removing South Korean labels and attaching Chinese ones, but that has become difficult as customs inspections have grown stricter,” the source said. “Recently, some have gone as far as transferring the contents of South Korean cosmetics into Chinese cosmetic containers and bringing them in disguised as Chinese products.”
Because it is difficult to confirm whether the contents are genuinely South Korean in such cases, there is also a risk that cheap Chinese cosmetics could be passed off as South Korean products and sold at inflated prices.
“Many of the wealthy buyers who order South Korean cosmetics have used the products for a long time, so they can tell to some extent by the scent, texture and feel,” the source said. “Merchants who have built trust with wealthy clients over years of business also have their livelihoods on the line, so it would not be easy for them to knowingly sell fakes.”
Sulwhasoo, a premium skincare brand from South Korea’s AmorePacific, and Gongjinhyang, a line from LG Household & Health Care’s luxury Whoo brand, are said to be especially popular among the North’s wealthy, with a set priced at 500 to 1,000 Chinese yuan, or about 100,000 to 200,000 South Korean won.
In China, brokers involved in trade with North Korea are reportedly transferring the contents of South Korean cosmetics into Chinese containers to fill North Korean orders.
“Customs crackdowns are intense, but North Korea keeps demanding South Korean cosmetics, so traders are buying Chinese cosmetic containers and South Korean cosmetics separately and transferring the contents themselves,” a China-based source who works with North Korea trade told Daily NK. “Foundation is especially difficult, though, because it’s hard to find containers of the right size, so traders struggle to transfer and send it.”
The source added, “If there were people who specialized in this work, they could earn money and save the traders effort, but no such specialists exist yet, so traders are doing the work themselves. No matter how much North Korea strengthens its crackdown, there will always be buyers, so the methods for evading inspection keep evolving.”

items.title: Richmond denies players 'making light' of Swans scandal on Mad Monday
items.summary: The Richmond Football Club says players were not "referencing or making light of recent matters" in videos circulating from the team's post-season celebrations.
items.body_text:
The Richmond Football Club says players were not "referencing or making light of recent matters" in videos circulating from the team's post-season celebrations.
Media camped outside the venue filmed players spanking each other on the rear.
The venue that hosted the Tigers for their Mad Monday drinks has lauded them for being "extremely respectful".
The Richmond Football Club has denied its players were "referencing or making light of recent matters" in footage recorded during their post-season celebrations.
Tiger players were recorded during a drinking session at a Victorian country pub, with one player seen feigning shock after being spanked on his rear by a teammate.
Another teammate whips a fellow player on the back with a belt in footage captured by news outlets on Monday, leading to speculation they were referencing the ongoing Sydney Swans scandal.
The club denied that was the case.
"Richmond is aware of a video circulating from a player end of season gathering," a statement read.
"The club has spoken to the players who have expressed their embarrassment over their behaviour.
"The players are adamant they were in no way referencing or making light of recent matters."
The Tigers finished second last this season with a 3-20 win-loss record.
The pub that hosted Richmond's drinks said the controversy had been blown out of proportion.
"In our view, this has been blown out of proportion," the Garfield Hotel, 80 kilometres east of Melbourne, said in a statement posted on social media.
The hotel said it "could not speak more highly" of how players behaved.
"For such a young group, they were extremely respectful and a fun group of boys to deal with," the statement read.
"They enjoyed a few quiet beers to unwind after a long season, and we see nothing wrong with that.
"They had booked out the venue for the afternoon, so they were the only patrons on site.
"They enjoyed their afternoon and moved on."
The hotel noted media were waiting for the Tigers players "in the hope of capturing a misstep, which we consider disappointing".
"I have been asked a lot in recent days, what message football should be sending young people and what we should be saying to our kids," Dillon said.
"For me, the answer is straightforward: it doesn't matter who you are, it doesn't matter what you do, whether you're an AFL footballer — the way we treat women says a lot about who we are as people, as a community and as a game.
"Quite simply, respect for women is not negotiable."
Dillon said the actions of the five suspended Swans players had "fallen well short of the standards our game expects and community deserves".
"While there are players involved, we cannot lose sight of the bigger picture. More importantly, there are women who have made a report to police and they should be shown care and respect," he said.

items.title: NRL changes rules to allow Jai Arrow to 'play' 100 games for Souths
items.summary: The Rabbitohs successfully petition the NRL to change the league's interchange rules to allow Jai Arrow to take the field for his 99th and 100th games for South Sydney in the last two rounds of the year.
items.body_text:
The NRL has changed its interchange rules to allow Jai Arrow to start the Rabbitohs' final two games of the 2026 regular season, taking him to 100 games for South Sydney.
The 31-year-old Arrow was forced to medically retire after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease.
What's next?
The Rabbitohs finish the regular season against Arrow's former club, the Titans, on the Gold Coast, before a clash with rivals the Roosters in Sydney.
Jai Arrow will make cameo appearances in the final two rounds of the regular season in order to reach 100 games for South Sydney.
In one of the feel-good stories of the NRL season, the forward who retired with motor neurone disease in May has been approved to start on the field in rounds 26 and 27.
Arrow will then be substituted out in the opening seconds before any active involvement in play.
Arrow, in jersey number 23, has been named co-captain with Cameron Murray, who is listed to come off the bench.
It came after the Rabbitohs made an appeal to the NRL to grant the former Queensland representative an on-field swansong while still able to walk and run.
The initiative gives Arrow two final chances to farewell an NRL career that featured a grand-final appearance in 2021 and 12 State of Origin caps.
The NRL has granted Souths special dispensation to name Arrow as an extra player on today's team list and an extra substitution in their rotation.
The matches, against Gold Coast and the Sydney Roosters, will bring Arrow's tally to 180 career games and 100 for the Rabbitohs.
Arrow will lead the team out on both occasions and sit on the interchange bench in Souths kit after being substituted out.
The Titans and Roosters have both approved the plan, as have the Rugby League Players Association.
"We are very grateful to Peter [V'landys] and the NRL, and Clint [Newton] at the RLPA, for supporting our proposal," Souths chief executive Blake Solly said.
"We believe this will provide great inspiration for everyone watching the game from the stadium or at home, showing that MND will not hold Jai, or anyone else, back from achieving what they want to achieve in life."
The NRL world has rallied around Arrow since his shock diagnosis and immediate retirement in May.
The league threw Arrow "the world's biggest birthday party" on the day Souths beat Newcastle in July, rolling out a birthday cake in the shape of the 31-year-old's jersey and presenting him with a commemorative jersey.
Fundraising efforts have already passed $1 million in support of Arrow, who is the father of a young daughter.
Players from all clubs have shown their support by marking tries with arrow celebrations throughout the month of July.

Essendon opens doors to James Hird return despite coaching snub in favour of Mark McVeigh
Posted , updated 
Essendon's new coach Mark McVeigh and president Andrew Welsh are set to speak with James Hird about a role at the club.
Welsh said his two phone calls to Hird after McVeigh's announcement went unanswered on Monday night, while McVeigh said he spoke to his former captain on Tuesday morning.
It remains to be seen whether Hird will be interested in a different role outside of head coach. McVeigh is expected to put together his coaching staff in the coming months, while there are also several roles in Essendon's football department that need filling.
New Essendon coach Mark McVeigh says he will speak to James Hird about returning to the club in a different capacity after a second failed bid to be coach.
McVeigh was unveiled on Tuesday in a press conference that was also attended by a number of Essendon's current players.
Both he and club president Andrew Welsh indicated their desire to have Hird involved.
"I'd love to see James as a part of the club going forward. He's such a fantastic football person," Welsh said.
Loading Twitter content
"I feel there's significant value James can bring, not just tokenistic, but real value to our club and our playing group.
"Certainly, part of my messaging was that Mark and I would want to catch up with him when the time is appropriate."
While Welsh said a pair of calls to Hird had gone unanswered on Monday night, McVeigh said he had shared a conversation with his former captain.
"I love James Hird, he's one of my best mates. It was difficult to go through the process against a good friend," he said.
"I don't fear those people [Hird's supporters], I actually embrace how they feel, and I understand it, to be fair.

Powerful Labor mayor takes swing over ‘half-hearted’ NSW gambling reforms
Updated ,first published
A powerful Sydney Labor mayor has criticised the Minns government’s gambling reforms as a “half-hearted” attempt to deal with the poker machine addiction, and vowed to keep up the pressure on his own party before the 2027 election.
Inner West Mayor Darcy Byrne’s comments came after Gaming Minister David Harris said the rollout of mandatory facial-recognition technology in pubs and clubs and a statewide gambling self-exclusion register means cutting the number of poker machines in the state would “make no difference at all”.
Nearly two years after an independent panel was convened to oversee the trial of cashless poker machines, the government has also ignored calls to introduce obligatory account-based gaming, instead saying it would begin exploring a system of opt-in “account-based” gambling.
The government on Tuesday announced the latest tranche of its gambling reforms, including a statewide exclusion register that would allow families, friends, police or venues to initiate bans for problem gamblers in hotels and clubs.
The announcement is unlikely to assuage critics of the government’s response to poker machines. Last month Premier Chris Minns faced an internal revolt at Labor’s state conference, with a cross-factional deal foisting more significant reforms on the government.
This included the absence of key elements of a deal negotiated by senior Labor figures at the party’s state conference in July.
A motion adopted unanimously by Labor members called for a new tax on Sydney’s richest clubs, which are responsible for the vast bulk of the $10 billion in poker machine losses recorded in NSW each year.
The motion also called for a “significant reduction” in the total number of pokies, a compromise agreed to with the government after senior figures from the Left and Right factions had pushed for a reduction of between 25,000 and 45,000 machines.
Byrne, a senior figure in Labor’s Left faction who was integral to the negotiation of the gambling reform deal, criticised the “half-hearted approach to addressing poker machine harm”, saying pressure for “real reform” would intensify ahead of the 2027 NSW election.
“Labor members voted for a ‘significant reduction’ in poker machines, but based on current trends, this plan would lead to just a few hundred of NSW’s 87,000 machines being decommissioned each year,” he said in a statement.
‘The fact that the poker machine lobby has not mounted a major campaign against these changes tells you everything you need to know.’Darcy Byrne, Inner West mayor
“The fact that the poker machine lobby has not mounted a major campaign against these changes tells you everything you need to know about how limited they are.”
While Harris said he was discussing taxation changes with Treasurer Daniel Mookhey, he appeared to walk away from using government policy to materially reduce the 87,000 pokies operating across about 2100 venues in NSW.
“That becomes less important once the technology is in play,” Harris said.
“The most important thing is that when a person is sitting at a machine anywhere in the state, they can set how long they can play. They can set how much they can spend. Once those things are in place, the actual number of machines matters less.
The rollout of mandatory facial-recognition technology is a major win for the clubs lobby, which has long campaigned for its use, instead of mandatory account-based or cashless gambling.
Stu Cameron, the chief executive of Wesley Mission, said clubs had been “pushing for this for ages”. He was concerned about how the rules would govern its use, including whether clubs could use data from the technology for things such as marketing. The Herald has previously revealed some companies that sell the technology to clubs promote it as a tool to “balance commerce and compliance” by identifying potential repeat customers.

items.title: Gambling reform package is a loss disguised as a win
items.summary: The government’s reforms do no harm but fall far short of addressing the social harms caused by poker machines.
items.body_text:
Gambling reform package is a loss disguised as a win
There is a particular feature of poker machine play that raises the pulses of reform advocates and gamblers alike, known as “losses disguised as wins”. The lights flash and the bells ring and the machine celebrates the spin like a win, but the payout is less than the amount wagered.
Depending how far you wind back the time machine on this state’s slow descent into poker machine addiction, the Minns government’s long-awaited gambling reform package could be described as a loss disguised as a win. There is nothing terrible about the measures announced on Tuesday. It’s a grab-bag of things that can’t hurt, things that might work and things that are long overdue.
But it goes nowhere near addressing the social harms that have emerged as a result of NSW having the highest number of poker machines per person in the world.
Starting with that metric, for example, the package includes an increased forfeiture rate when gaming machine entitlements are traded, from one in three to one in two, so that for every two entitlements traded, one machine is permanently removed from circulation. This is designed to reduce the number of poker machines over time.
NSW has about 87,000 poker machines. That is just 13,758 fewer than when the forfeiture scheme was introduced 25 years ago. The NSW Audit Office projected last year it would take 55 years to reach parity with the national average. The accelerated forfeiture rate might shave a decade off that time frame, but only if pubs and clubs do not change their behaviour. They might decide the forfeiture rate is too high and stop transferring their entitlements altogether.
The second big item is a statewide third-party exclusion scheme for people experiencing gambling harm. Gambling harm advocates have long advocated for this. Previously, people could ask to be excluded from particular venues, but there was nothing to stop them going elsewhere to get their gambling fix. Few will object to that loophole being closed, or the new ability for third parties to intervene to place their loved ones on the exclusion register.
Similarly, the strengthened protections against harmful gambling advertising, a ban on VIP programs that reward high rollers, a ban on gambling advertising on government-owned buildings, and new transparency requirements for influencers can only reduce gambling harm.
But when it comes to poker machines being used for money laundering – that is, criminals using them to disguise the origins of dirty cash – the changes fall far short.
A casual observer might forget the NSW Crime Commission’s damning 2023 report into money laundering in pubs and clubs was the original catalyst for gambling reform. That problem has not gone away. The financial crimes watchdog last year launched civil proceedings against the state’s largest club group, Mounties, for allegedly allowing criminals to launder $226 million through its pokies.
The independent panel for gaming reform recommended last year the government introduce mandatory account-based gaming, which would require gamblers to provide identification and allow crime agencies to track their transactions.
This top-line recommendation has appeared only in ghost form. Under these reforms, the government will upgrade the Centralised Monitoring System over the next two years to allow venues to transition to account-based play, which will give players the option of playing without cash – but it will not be mandatory.
Setting aside the fact they could have done this two years ago, a voluntary, ad hoc system will do nothing to reduce money laundering. Instead, the government has committed to introducing mandatory facial recognition technology at the entrance to gaming rooms – the money laundering prevention method favoured by the gambling industry – and this will also support the statewide exclusion program.

items.title: ‘Enough is enough’: 121 Indigenous Victorians have died by suicide in the past five years
items.summary: Royal commission recommended First Nations healing centres in 2021 but the Indigenous health service says the state has ‘done nothing’ to fund itFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastOn the steps of Victorian parliament stood 121 empty chairs, marking the number of Indigenous lives lost to suicide in the state in the past five years.All of these deaths, the state’s peak body for Aboriginal health said, came after the fina
items.body_text:
On the steps of Victorian parliament stood 121 empty chairs, marking the number of Indigenous lives lost to suicide in the state in the past five years.
All of these deaths, the state’s peak body for Aboriginal health said, came after the final report of the royal commission into mental health in March 2021.
Its key findings heavily emphasised Aboriginal self-determination, social and emotional wellbeing, and the establishment of two cultural healing centres.
The state government accepted all 65 recommendations from the final report and nine from the interim report, but is yet to fully implement those directly related to First Nations people who remain three times more likely to die by suicide.
The Victorian Aboriginal Health Organisation (VACCHO) chief executive, Jill Gallagher, said the tragic statistic showed that mainstream mental health services are not working for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.
“A lot of recommendations came out of that report and not many Aboriginal recommendations have been implemented,” the Gunditjmara woman said. “The government has done nothing. We have not established those very important healing centres, and it is crucial to try and address those numbers.
“These aren’t just figures we’re talking about, these are members of our families. Our families suffer, our communities suffer.”
Gallagher said VACCHO had applied twice in the past five years to see the healing centres funded, with an estimated cost of $36.2m over four years.
Gunditjmara woman Nikki Foy, who lost her brother to suicide more than 20 years ago, said mainstream mental health services were not equipped to handle “complexities of the trauma that we carry”.
“We need healing centres that are culturally appropriate for our mob. Culture heals,” she said.
“Today, or tomorrow, some family out there will receive a phone call. A mother, a father, a brother, sister, uncle or aunty or grandparents will get that call and be told that their loved one has passed by suicide … enough is enough.
“We are the experts that know how to support and how to help our mob. Let us do that.”
Reducing rates of suicide in Indigenous communities is one of the 17 Closing the Gap targets.
Both the Victorian minister for mental health, Ingrid Stitt, and the opposition spokesperson, Emma Kealy, addressed reporters alongside Gallagher. But while both spoke of the need to address the self-harm crisis in Indigenous communities, neither committed to funding the centres.
The Coalition has vowed to repeal Victoria’s historic treaty laws and dismantle Gellung Warl, the representative body for First Nations Victorians set up within that treaty process, within 100 days if it wins the state election in November.
Asked if abolishing Gellung Warl would help reduce suicide rates, Kealy said the Coalition’s policy was focused on making sure Aboriginal community-controlled organisations were funded and said that “while the journey may be different”, the party was committed to closing the gap.
Stitt said she would continue to advocate “strongly within cabinet and within the budget process” to have the healing centre projects supported.
“Treaty is a huge part of this,” Stitt added.
“Proud First Nations peoples in Victoria have the solutions, and we will work really hard to make sure that they have the power to be able to deliver those solutions.”

items.title: Man denied parole a second time over anti-Israel graffiti despite judge’s scathing critique of case
items.summary: NSW parole authority says Mohommed Farhat followed ‘extremist ideology of antisemitic character’ while separately judge ruled ‘Fuk Israel’ was ‘political comment’Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastA Sydney man convicted of writing “Fuk Israel” on cars and setting another vehicle alight has had his release on parole rejected a second time, despite a supreme court judge stating the case appeared to be a “serious miscarri
items.body_text:
A Sydney man convicted of writing “Fuk Israel” on cars and setting another vehicle alight has had his release on parole rejected a second time, despite a supreme court judge stating the case appeared to be a “serious miscarriage of justice”.
Mohommed Farhat, 22, was initially due to be released on parole in December after serving 10 months in prison following the November 2024 vandalism in Woollahra.
But he remained behind bars after a rare intervention by the commissioner for corrective services, who then told the New South Wales parole authority at a hearing in March that Farhat’s offending showed support for “extremist” behaviour.
Last week, the supreme court justice Desmond Fagan delivered a scathing ruling after the state sought a supervision order for Farhat on his release from jail using the Terrorism Act.
Fagan found there was an “insignificant” risk that Farhat, who was of “limited intellect”, would commit a serious terrorism offence. He ruled the police, lower courts and various state agencies all incorrectly labelled Farhat’s actions antisemitic rather than “a curse against a foreign state”.
Fagan determined that Farhat, who has a Hezbollah tattoo on his neck, was treated more harshly than he should have been after he pleaded guilty to 15 offences in connection with property damage.
The judge accepted Farhat was paid to undertake the vandalism and said the case appeared to be a “serious miscarriage of justice”.
On Wednesday last week, Fagan said he planned to write to the commissioner for the state’s parole authority ahead of an expected decision on Farhat’s potential release following the March hearing.
The parole authority then handed down its decision on Monday, five months after the hearing. It did not consider Fagan’s findings or evidence that counter-terrorism police determined three weeks after Farhat was arrested that he was not ideologically motivated.
The authority’s decision to keep the 22-year-old in prison stated: “In the authority’s view, the offending was reflective of a deep-seated adherence on the part of the offender to an extremist ideology of an antisemitic character.”
The authority rejected Farhat’s explanation, accepted by Fagan, that he was paid to carry out the vandalism.
“Further, the authority does not accept the offender’s claimed ignorance of the meaning of the phrases which were used in the offending,” the parole authority wrote.
On Monday, the commissioner for corrective services, Gary McMahon, was questioned about Farhat’s case in budget estimates and his rare intervention in December, when he successfully applied to have Farhat’s parole order revoked without hearing from his lawyers. A fresh hearing date was then set for March.
People sentenced to less than three years in jail are typically released on parole when it comes due.

items.title: Trump administration expands U.S. sanctions on Iran targeting countries with business ties to Tehran
items.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump's administration on Monday announced an expansion of secondary sanctions it can impose on ‌entities and countries that maintain business ties with Iran around the world, as Washington significantly ratchets up economic pressure on Tehran with the war nearing its six-month mark.
items.body_text:
Trump administration expands U.S. sanctions on Iran targeting countries with business ties to Tehran
Treasury says it has mapped the networks Iran uses to smuggle oil and evade sanctions
U.S. President Donald Trump's administration on Monday announced an expansion of secondary sanctions it can impose on entities and countries that maintain business ties with Iran, significantly ratcheting up economic pressure on Tehran as the war nears its six-month mark.
At a press conference, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled what he described as an "economic D-Day" aimed at giving countries a final warning to sever business ties with Iran or risk having key companies and entities cut off from the dollar-based financial system.
"We are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe. Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," Bessent said.
The U.S. Treasury Department said it has mapped the networks, facilitators and financial channels Iran uses to smuggle oil and evade sanctions, and that Washington would work with U.S. partners to target any source of Iran's "illicit revenue."
The department said it has issued determinations against five sectors — digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping — that the Iranian government uses to prop up its economy. The Treasury has also imposed sanctions on nearly 60 entities, individuals and vessels.
China has for several years been the biggest buyer of Iranian oil. Washington has intensified efforts to clamp down on Chinese purchases but has so far stopped short of designating larger Chinese banks that may be facilitating the trade.
'Wait for an attack,' Iran warns
Before the announcement, Iran threatened both a possible military response and further reduction in oil exports from the Gulf in response to any U.S. economic measures.
Afterward, Iranian Finance and Economic Affairs Minister Ali Madanizadeh said, "We are fully prepared for the U.S. sanctions."
"Naturally, the enemies intend to launch an economic terrorist attack on us, but we also have our own tools and know how to play the game. Our defence is no longer so defensive; the enemies should wait for an attack," Madanizadeh told state television.
Brig-Gen. Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), vowed heavy blows to U.S. vital interests and energy chokepoints if Iran's infrastructure is threatened, Press TV reported.
The war between the U.S. and Iran is nearing the six-month mark and has pushed energy prices higher worldwide. While heavy fighting has subsided, diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have stalled, and oil and raw-material shipments through the Strait of Hormuz remain blocked, keeping energy prices elevated.
Trump's approval rating has fallen to a low point, with just 33 per cent of Americans in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll approving of his performance. He says the economic costs are necessary to ensure Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon.
The U.S. has maintained sanctions against Iran for decades. Most have been aimed at curtailing the country's oil revenues, targeting its aviation sector and cryptocurrency activity, restricting its procurement of weapons components and other military hardware, and cutting off funding for business enterprises controlled by the IRGC, a dominant force in the Iranian economy.
The sanctions bar designated entities from the dollar-based financial system, but Iran has been successful in quickly standing up new front companies, entities and vessel registrations to evade them.

items.body_text:
London is famous for its great trees. More than 70% are at risk due to climate change, research finds
Heat waves and drought in the U.K. are putting stress on London's trees
In the middle of a heat wave and severe drought in Britain this summer, Divya Hariramani was pruning a plum tree in south London when she noticed something wrong with one of the tree's branches.
The branch was beginning to split completely from the tree. The workers at Mitcham Community Orchard told her it was because the fruit tree was stressed.
"Because of the heat essentially. Like, when the trees can't provide enough water to its parts and like some parts will just drop," said Hariramani, who documents fruit trees and the people who tend to them across the city on a social media account called Fruity Walks.
While London’s stone architecture may be more famous to some tourists, the 2,000-year-old city is also renowned for its mature urban forest, which has been called the largest in the world.
This year has proven difficult for the normally lush canopy, though, as five successive heat waves and a serious lack of rain have strained plants and wildlife.
And it’s projected to get much worse for the city’s eight million trees.
By the end of the century, according to a recent report from Royal Botanic Gardens Kew forecasting the vulnerability of London’s urban forest, some 73 per cent of the city’s trees could be at risk of dying due to climate change.
Driest July on record
The Kew Gardens tree collections and arboriculture team worked with the Greater London Authority to assess a sample of over a million public trees and found that 62 per cent of them already have "low suitability" to the climate conditions that can be expected by 2090 without action to reduce emissions. On top of that, nearly 11 per cent are “vulnerable."
It’s not just a future problem. In 2022, 400 of Kew's 11,000 trees died amid extreme heat and drought conditions. The gardens have left the skeleton of one red oak standing, and painted it red as a symbol of what climate change is already doing to London's trees.
Kew highlighted the findings and unveiled the red tree ahead of Climate Action Week in June, when Britain and Europe were already in the throes of a second heat wave. By August, there had been two more and a major drought was declared in much of England and Wales. Virtually no rain fell in July, resulting in the driest July on record in Britain.
Farmers lost crops, warned of food shortages and had to dip into winter feed reserves for cattle. Wildfires in parts of the country prompted an emergency cellphone alert in August. In the city, park grass turned yellow and brittle; tree branches and leaves looked droopier than usual. In some places, trees lost their leaves altogether, giving an autumnal look to the ground in the middle of summer.
The week in June when Kew publicized its report, Hariramani, in an ironic twist of fate, had to cancel a group walk she had organized in light of Climate Action Week due to the heat.
"Literally one of the most important walks in a way, for such an important situation and we couldn't even do it," said Hariramani, whose day job is in sustainable design.
More like Barcelona?
With a London that’s getting warmer than its current trees can handle, botanists are exploring whether they should start planting different trees.
"From most projections, we're expecting the climate in London in 2050 to look more like Barcelona's is now," Joe Richomme, a botanical horticulturist at Kew Gardens, told CBC on a recent visit to Kew’s Carbon Garden, where 35 trees and 6,500 plants have been selected to show how different species respond to changing conditions.
Richomme explained that Kew has been exploring what types of tree species could fare better in hotter, drier weather, while also being able to withstand England’s notorious wetter winters.

items.summary: European leaders joined President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on Monday for official celebrations marking Ukraine's Independence Day as Russia pushes on with its invasion of the country.
items.body_text:
U.K. to provide long-range missile blueprints to Ukraine
New PM expected to announce release of SCALP missile plans, office says
European leaders joined President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on Monday for official celebrations marking Ukraine's Independence Day as Russia pushes on with its invasion of the country.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, on his first overseas trip since taking office last month, on Monday joined almost a dozen other European leaders, as well as other dignitaries including European Council President Antonio Costa, in Kyiv.
"For Ukraine, independence is not an abstract idea. We defended it against all odds," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media. "In times like these, nations learn how important it is to have allies by your side." Ukrainians voted overwhelmingly for independence in 1991, but one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's key goals in starting a war in February 2022 was to place Kyiv in Moscow's orbit.
Burnham co-chaired a meeting of the so-called Coalition of the Willing group of countries helping Ukraine resist Russia's onslaught, with the leaders of France and Germany expected to join online.
Burnham said he is pushing British industry to help a Ukrainian project that is working on a low-cost alternative to the U.S.-made Patriot air defence systems that Zelenskyy has said Ukraine desperately needs but are in short supply. Burnham urged other countries to encourage Washington to adopt stiffer sanctions on Russia and press Moscow to accept U.S. attempts to secure an unconditional ceasefire.
The visiting leaders took to Kyiv pledges of further military and financial support.
Burnham is expected to announce that the U.K. government has agreed to allow defence company MBDA to release classified information relating to British components used in the SCALP long-range missile, according to his office. That would pave the way for France and Ukraine to advance plans for local production of the weapon in Ukraine.
SCALP is the French version of the U.K.'s Storm Shadow missile, with both systems incorporating shared French and British technology.
"We all understand that in this Russian war against us — against Ukraine — far more is being decided than the future of Ukraine and Eastern Europe," Zelenskyy said, adding that foreign help was vital.
"No nation in a war like this could rely solely on its own weapons," he said. "No nation could withstand attacks of such intensity without the world's help."
'Fuel to the fire'
The Kremlin said Britain's decision was regarded by Moscow extremely negatively.
"Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire and methodically and regularly hatches schemes to prevent even the slightest progress in the peaceful settlement process," spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
Peskov said that the Russian military was already systematically gathering data to identify the location of any missile production sites and then destroying them.
Moscow warned London last week of unspecified "consequences" for supplying drones to Kyiv, accusing Britain of deepening its involvement in the war following a report that British-made drones had been used for long-range strikes against Russia for the first time.
Burnham said at the time that London was committed to support Ukraine fully against "this illegal war."
Ukraine has leaned heavily on NATO countries for help fighting Russia's bigger army, although relations with the United States have been cooler under Donald Trump than predecessor Joe Biden. Trump said at a NATO summit last month that the U.S. would give Ukraine a licence to produce Patriot missiles, but there has been no further announcement since. Even with a licence, officials and experts told The Associated Press that starting Patriot production in Ukraine would take years.
Russia, meanwhile, is getting help from North Korea and China while having made use of Iran's Shahed drone

items.title: Trump’s trade war threatens Republicans in key U.S. Senate races
items.summary: Republicans in states with close economic ties to Canada are facing pressure as the trade dispute intensifies
items.body_text:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada is escalating as the midterm elections approach, threatening Republican efforts to address voters’ economic concerns in a year when control of the U.S. Senate hinges on states along the border between the United States and its northern neighbour.
The dispute flared over the weekend after negotiations broke down, leading Trump to raise tariffs on $28-billion in Canadian imports. Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada plans to announce tariffs of its own on Tuesday. The spiralling conflict could lead to higher prices and scrambled supply chains for Americans already aggravated at the president’s management of the economy.
Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, one of Democrats’ top targets this year, warned that fallout from Trump’s approach would hurt U.S. businesses and consumers.
“Imposing new tariffs on Canada is a mistake,” Collins said while campaigning Monday, and she mentioned lobsters, blueberries, lumber and other Maine products that end up in Canadian markets.
Canada won’t return to negotiating table until U.S. changes its attitude, Carney says
The issue also puts pressure on Republicans in Michigan, Ohio and Alaska, states where Canada is an important trading partner. Many Democrats seem eager to capitalize on the matter as they try to regain the Senate majority, despite the party’s own history with protectionist sentiments.
“Trump is escalating a trade war with Canada for his own vanity,” Michigan’s Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed said on social media, adding that his Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, is a “rubber stamp” for such policies. A third of the state’s exports go north of the border.
Marc Short, a top adviser to then-Vice President Mike Pence during the first Trump presidency, said the issue is a political trap for Republicans.
“It’s hard, obviously, because you don’t want to incur the wrath of the president,” he said. “But at the same time, I think if you’re representing agricultural states, especially, your voters are probably anxious to have somebody representing their interests in Washington right now.”
Trump charges forward on tariffs
It’s possible that Trump will change course or delay his plans. But for now, the president is making no apologies for the economic turmoil.
“Canada has been ripping off the United States for years,” Trump blasted on his Truth Social platform Monday, adding that he will raise tariffs on all Canadian automobiles and auto parts and steel to 50% in 2027. He added, “WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!”
Trump’s top trade official more calmly played down the dispute. “This is something where we don’t actually expect a huge impact,” U.S. Trade Rep. Jamieson Greer told reporters outside the West Wing.
Ottawa faces dilemma as it weighs how to hit back at U.S. over tariffs
U.S. Vice President JD Vance visited Maine on Monday, where he praised “our very independent friend Susan Collins” and assured voters “we’re very mindful of the fact that Maine is a border state with Canada.” He said the administration is trying to make sure Maine “gets a fair deal.”
Collins did not appear with Vance on Monday or during his last trip to Maine. She campaigned on her own as she tries to hold off a challenge from Democratic nominee Troy Jackson, a former state legislative leader.
Jackson, a logger before going into politics, said tariffs are another example of how Collins does not do enough to stand up to the president.
“Troy spent most of his life working along the Canadian border, so he knows how important this relationship is to Maine’s economy,” Jackson spokesman Dan Gottlieb said.
Republicans are trying to defend Senate control
Trump made no secret of his affection for tariffs during his comeback campaign, promising that higher taxes on imports would generate a windfall for the U.S. Treasury and boost domestic manufacturing. But concerns about inflation and affordability have not receded, including in states with key races this

items.title: Americans, too, are wondering why the U.S. and Canada are embroiled in a trade war
items.summary: Thirteen American states border Canada and have a stake in the relationship
items.body_text:
Nine centuries ago, the theologian Moses Maimonides, seeking to understand the complexities of life, wrote a volume called The Guide for the Perplexed.
Those searching for wisdom on the state of the Canada-U.S. relationship after the abrupt break in bilateral trade negotiations surely are perplexed – but have no guide.
Nearly two decades ago, the WB Television Network created a TV drama called Jack & Bobby in which there were fleeting but troubling references to a mysterious future conflict called the “War of the Americas.” No one in the period in which that show aired – Paul Martin was prime minister – could have taken the notion seriously, and certainly no one would have imagined that when a prime minister in 2026 spoke of Canada being at war, the opponent would be the United States.
Trump revives annexation comments as governors warn tariffs on Canada will harm Americans
Mark Carney – who said “Canada is becoming stronger and less dependent on America” – surely meant the word “war” metaphorically, as in the phrase American philosopher William James employed in a famous 1910 speech, “The Moral Equivalent of War,” or in relation to the trade war that has been simmering since Donald Trump’s first term, only to break into wildfire flames in recent days.
The two countries aren’t in a conflict like the India-Pakistan hostilities that have flared for three-quarters of a century. It’s more like the Anglo-Dutch trade fight of the 17th century, though this one involves two countries that were, since the years leading up to the Second World War until the middle of the last decade, allies arguably without precedent in the history of humankind.
Now, the question is whether this is a permanent break or merely another temporary but significant episode like the two countries’ long-ago military conflicts: the 1775 invasion of Quebec, the War of 1812 and the Fenian raids of 1866 and 1870-1871. History suggests that while Mr. Carney is right that Canada’s ties to the United States are now in a different form, they have not been severed completely.
“This isn’t the end of anything,” said Christopher Ragan, the emeritus McGill University economist and author of Canada’s most widely used postsecondary economics textbook. “It’s the beginning of another policy tantrum from Donald Trump. He wanted a political win and didn’t get it. And the question now may be: If he can’t deal with little Canada, what can he do? But this shows we’re not prepared to cave to American pressure.”
Premiers present united front behind Carney, but divisions emerge on next steps
Prof. Ragan said this episode may be a symbolic turn to a world in which countries everywhere grow more protectionist.
“If you care about your industries and supply chains, you may have to pay an economic price,” he said. “If we’re going to diversify our trade away from the U.S., there may be a price to pay. But it may lead to more economic security for us all.”
It’s clear large segments of the U.S. political world are troubled by this development.
Thirteen American states border Canada and have a stake in Canada-U.S. trade and tourism. The reaction was swift from several political figures from those border states.
“Canada is not our enemy – any suggestion otherwise is ridiculous,” Republican Governor Phil Scott of Vermont said. “At a time of growing economic and geopolitical uncertainty, the United States should be strengthening this partnership, not weakening it.”
Democratic Senator Patty Murray of Washington, a state where Canada is the largest trade partner, said in a social-media post that “Trump owes our friends and neighbours an apology for nearly 2 years of his boorish insults and jeers.” Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul of New York spoke of the President “needlessly picking fights with our allies and raising prices here at home.”
